title: The thread on your wrist
hookLine: a coworker asks about the red thread on your wrist, and the demon king its verse remembers
carry: raksha: a thread that asks God to protect you

lines: A VERSE, SAID AS IT'S TIED.
cards: A coworker notices it while you're both waiting for coffee: a red and yellow thread, a little faded, tied around your wrist. Is that a friendship bracelet? Not quite.
A priest tied it at a puja weeks ago, and while he tied it he said a short Sanskrit verse. The verse names a king. His name was Bali.
He was a demon king, he had conquered heaven itself, and he was well-known for one thing: he never refused anyone a gift.

teach.b: Here's his story, as the Bhagavata tells it.

The gods had lost heaven to Bali, so Vishnu came to his sacrifice as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for a gift: just three steps of land. Bali's own teacher warned him it was a trick. Bali gave anyway.
Then the small boy grew until one step covered the earth and the next the heavens. No room was left for a third. So Bali bowed and offered his own head.
He was bound, and he lost his kingdom. But the story doesn't end there. Vishnu, moved by a king who kept his word, gave him a world of his own and promised to stay near him and protect him.
Many families hear the verse this way: the one who was bound became the one God guards. That's the verse at your wrist.
As the priest ties the kalava, a raksha sutra, a protection thread, he says, in effect: with the thread that bound mighty Bali, I bind you; protection, hold firm. Raksha means protection.
The thread is a prayer, tied on, asking God to look after you.
The black dot on a baby's cheek is a cousin: kajal against nazar, the evil eye, the fear that even loving admiration can harm something new, so a small flaw goes on purpose.
That one's a folk custom, not scripture; families keep it seriously, with a smile, or not at all. Your coffee-line answer: it's a protection thread. Someone tied it on me with a prayer.

how: Many priests tie a red and yellow kalava thread on the wrist at the end of a puja, often saying a verse that names King Bali; many families put a small dot of kajal on a baby against nazar, the evil eye, and some shops hang a lemon and seven green chilies by the door.

o: a lucky charm that keeps good fortune at home
a curse cast on purpose by someone who hates you
a look: the evil eye that too much praise can bring

games.q: the thread and its story — tap the pairs.
p: the demon king who kept his word
Vishnu as the boy who asked for three steps
a raksha sutra, a protection thread

s: the kalava thread is only for brothers on Raksha Bandhan
a priest or an elder can tie it on anyone at the end of a puja.
the verse said while tying the kalava names King Bali
with the thread that bound mighty Bali, I bind you; protection, hold firm.
the black dot against nazar is a command in the old scriptures
it's a loved folk custom. some families keep it seriously, some with a smile, some not at all.

games.q: you're King Bali. your own teacher warns you the little boy-priest asking for three steps is Vishnu, and it's a trick. what does the story say you do?
o: take back your promise. a trick cancels it.
keep your word and give the three steps.
give two steps and keep the rest.
games.why: Bali gave anyway, and lost his kingdom. then Vishnu promised to stay near him and protect him: bound, then guarded. that's the binding the thread remembers.

practice: Rest your attention on your wrist, as if a thread were tied there, and think of someone who has looked out for you, out loud or quietly: tied a thread, said a prayer, waited up until you got home.
Let the feeling sit on your skin for a few breaths. If you pray, ask God's protection over them, the way the priest asked it over you; if you don't, simply send them your thanks.

wordCard.voice: Nazar. A look: the evil eye that families ward off with a black dot. The thread asks for raksha; the dot keeps off nazar. Today's word.

orig.note: Hindi and Urdu, from Arabic: a look, a glance; the evil eye.

carryVoice: Your line: raksha, a thread that asks God to protect you. Bound like Bali, and guarded like him. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.18–8.23 (Vamana asks Bali for three steps; Shukra warns him; Bali keeps his word and offers his head; he is bound, then given Sutala, and Vishnu promises to stay near and protect him)

sources.work: Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English (1884)

sources.ref: kalava / raksha sutra tied at the close of puja (often with the verse 'yena baddho bali raja')
kajal dot and nimbu-mirchi against nazar
